grapefruit.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8's cooler, higher pockets of the region see winter lows well below grapefruit's mid-20s°F wood- and fruit-damage threshold in an ordinary year, so there is no dependable in-ground establishment window here. Grapefruit also carries the highest summer-heat requirement of the common citrus, but that never comes into play: winter cold decides the case first.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for a grapefruit tree outside. This is the coolest part of the Nevada high desert, and winters regularly drop past the point that damages both the tree and the fruit.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Ordinary winter lows in this zone sit well past grapefruit's mid-20s°F damage point; a hard freeze is the rule here, not an occasional event.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley floor sits close to grapefruit's mid-20s°F wood- and fruit-damage threshold: University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) notes valley winter nights run colder than the Phoenix low desert floor, so grapefruit does not earn the fruits-reliably verdict it gets in Arizona's low desert. A container tree brought fully under cover, or indoors, on hard-freeze nights can persist here for years, but this is a protected specimen, not a dependable in-ground or fruiting planting.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit does not do well outdoors in the Las Vegas Valley. Our winter nights run colder than Phoenix's, so this does not fruit reliably the way it does in the Arizona desert. Grow it in a large pot you bring under cover on cold nights, and do not expect a steady crop.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The valley's frost season (last freeze around Feb 28, first around Nov 25, NWS Las Vegas normals) brackets a winter cold enough, on its harder nights, to reach past grapefruit's mid-20s°F damage point most years.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Laughlin/Colorado River corner is the region's mildest pocket, and its ordinary winter lows mostly clear grapefruit's mid-20s°F damage threshold. Even so, this is a single small area with no dedicated local citrus field data, and a periodic harder freeze can still reach past that point, so a protected container tree, not an in-ground planting, stays the honest call here too.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin is the warmest corner of the region, and grapefruit has its best shot here, but it is still not a sure thing. Keep it in a container you can protect on the coldest nights rather than planting it in the ground.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Even the region's mildest corner sees an occasional harder freeze that can reach grapefruit's mid-20s°F damage point; a movable container is the safer bet.

grapefruit.region_notes_beginner: Grapefruit is one of the toughest calls in this region: skip it outdoors everywhere except a sheltered container at the mild Laughlin corner, and even there do not count on a real harvest. Las Vegas Valley winters run colder than Phoenix's, so this does not behave like the reliable Arizona-desert grapefruit tree. Bring a container tree fully under cover on cold nights.
grapefruit.region_notes_seasoned: Grapefruit is cold-limited across the whole Nevada high desert, more so than in the Arizona low desert: University of Nevada, Reno Extension field evidence (SP-20-07) notes the Las Vegas Valley's winter nights run colder than Phoenix's valley floor, so this crop does not clone Phoenix's fruits-reliably verdict here. The cooler zone-8 pockets rule it out outright. The Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) and even the milder Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) sit close to grapefruit's mid-20s°F wood- and fruit-damage threshold, so a protected, fully-covered container tree is the realistic ceiling everywhere in this belt, not a dependable in-ground or fruiting planting. Summer heat is never the constraint; winter cold decides the case.
grapefruit.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 30 to 40°F in the mild Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) to 20 to 30°F in the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) to 10 to 20°F in the region's cooler, higher pockets (zone 8). Grapefruit takes wood and fruit damage around the mid-20s°F, so only the mildest zones sit close to that edge, and University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) documents Las Vegas Valley winter nights running colder than the Phoenix low desert floor, the reason this crop is judged more cold-limited here than in Arizona's low desert.
grapefruit.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here get cold enough, in every part of the region, to threaten a grapefruit tree, and our valley floor is colder at night than Phoenix's. The mild corner near Laughlin is the closest thing to a safe spot, and even that needs a protected container, not in-ground planting.
grapefruit.heat_basis_seasoned: The Nevada high desert's long, intensely hot, dry summer, routinely above 90 to 100°F (University of Nevada, Reno Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), would bank ample heat to sweeten grapefruit, the citrus with the highest summer-heat need, if the tree could reliably clear winter. Heat is not the limiting factor anywhere in this region; winter cold is.
grapefruit.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers are plenty hot for grapefruit. Winter cold, not summer heat, is what keeps this from being a reliable in-ground tree here.

lemon.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8's cooler, higher pockets bring winter lows well below the high-20s°F point where true lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is damaged, and even below the low-to-mid 20s°F tolerance of the hardier Improved Meyer hybrid. There is no in-ground establishment window this far into the region's cold edge; grow it as a container tree brought fully indoors for winter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for a lemon tree outside, even the hardier Meyer type. Grow one in a pot you bring fully indoors for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze most winters in this zone reaches well past even Improved Meyer's cold tolerance, let alone true lemon's.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley floor sits close to the edge for the hardiest lemon option: Improved Meyer, a lemon x mandarin hybrid, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F, near this zone's colder nights. University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) notes the valley runs colder at night than the Phoenix low desert, so lemon does not fruit reliably here the way it can in Arizona. A container Meyer brought fully under cover on hard-freeze nights can persist for years, but this stays a protected specimen, not a dependable in-ground or fruiting tree; true lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is more tender still and does not belong outdoors here at all.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The best lemon can do in the Las Vegas Valley is survive in a pot: Improved Meyer, the cold-hardy lemon type, can live for years if you bring it under cover on the coldest nights, but do not expect a real harvest. Regular lemon types are too tender to try here at all.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The valley's frost season (last freeze around Feb 28, first around Nov 25, NWS Las Vegas normals) brackets a winter whose harder nights reach past even Improved Meyer's low-to-mid 20s°F cold limit in most years.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Laughlin/Colorado River corner is the region's mildest pocket, and Improved Meyer's ordinary winter lows here mostly clear its low-to-mid 20s°F cold limit. This is still a single small area with no dedicated local citrus field data, and a periodic harder freeze can reach past that limit, so a protected container Meyer, not an in-ground tree, is the honest call; true lemon remains too tender to try even here.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin gives lemon its best shot in this region, with the hardy Meyer type, but keep it in a container you can protect rather than planting in the ground. Regular lemon is still too tender to try even in this warmer corner.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Even the region's mildest corner sees an occasional harder freeze that can reach Improved Meyer's low-to-mid 20s°F cold limit; a movable container is the safer bet.

lemon.region_notes_beginner: Regular lemon does not work outdoors anywhere in this region. The hardier Meyer type can survive in a container, brought under cover on cold nights, in the Las Vegas Valley and does a little better at the milder Laughlin corner, but do not count on a real harvest in either spot. The cooler high pockets of the region are too cold even for Meyer.
lemon.region_notes_seasoned: Lemon is not a landscape tree anywhere in the Nevada high desert. The region's cooler zone-8 pockets rule out even the hardiest selection. In the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) and the milder Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10), Improved Meyer, a naturally more cold-tolerant lemon x mandarin hybrid, sits close to its own low-to-mid 20s°F cold limit, so a container tree brought fully under cover for the coldest nights can be a long-lived planting, but not a fruiting one. University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) notes Las Vegas Valley winter nights run colder than the Phoenix low desert floor, the reason lemon is judged more cold-limited here than in Arizona's low desert. True lemon (Eureka, Lisbon) is more cold-tender still and is not a realistic choice outdoors anywhere in this region.
lemon.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 30 to 40°F in the mild Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) to 20 to 30°F in the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) to 10 to 20°F in the region's cooler, higher pockets (zone 8). True lemon is damaged in the high 20s°F and does not belong outdoors anywhere here; Improved Meyer, the hardier lemon x mandarin hybrid, tolerates cold into the low-to-mid 20s°F, the one real cold-edge option in the valley and Laughlin. University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) documents Las Vegas Valley winter nights running colder than the Phoenix low desert floor.
lemon.cold_basis_beginner: Regular lemon is too tender for this region. The hardier Meyer type can survive winter in a container in the Las Vegas Valley or the milder Laughlin corner if you protect it on cold nights, but even that needs help, and the cooler high pockets of the region are too cold for it too.

lime.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Lime is the most cold-tender common citrus: even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) type takes damage near 32°F, essentially at the freezing point, and this zone's cooler, higher pockets drop well past that on almost every winter night. There is no in-ground establishment window here at all; grow it as a container tree brought fully indoors for winter.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for a lime tree outside. Lime is hurt by cold more easily than almost any other citrus, damaged practically at freezing, and winters here regularly get colder than that. Grow it in a pot you bring fully indoors for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze every winter in this zone is well past lime's freezing-point damage threshold.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Even the Las Vegas Valley floor is too cold for lime in an ordinary winter: this zone's typical coldest nights, in the 20s°F, sit well below lime's roughly 32°F damage point, and University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) notes the valley runs colder at night than the Phoenix low desert, where lime is likewise the region's most cold-exposed citrus. There is no in-ground planting here; even a container specimen needs to come fully indoors, not just under cover, whenever a freeze threatens.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Lime does not work outdoors in the Las Vegas Valley either. It is damaged by cold that is barely below freezing, and our valley winters routinely get colder than that. Keep it as a houseplant you bring fully indoors for winter.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The valley's ordinary winter lows (last freeze around Feb 28, first around Nov 25, NWS Las Vegas normals) run well below lime's roughly 32°F damage threshold on its coldest nights.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Laughlin/Colorado River corner is the only part of this region where lime has a real chance: ordinary winter lows here mostly sit above lime's roughly 32°F damage point, so a well-protected container tree can survive. This is a single small area with no dedicated local citrus field data, and a periodic harder freeze can still dip into lime's damage range, so this stays a protected container prospect, never a dependable in-ground or fruiting tree; lime remains the most cold-exposed citrus in this batch even at its best Nevada location.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin is the one spot in this region where a potted lime has a real shot at surviving winter, but even there keep it in a container you can protect or bring indoors on cold nights. It is still the most cold-sensitive citrus tree.
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Even the region's mildest corner sees an occasional harder freeze that can reach lime's roughly 32°F damage threshold; keep the tree in a container you can move under full cover.

lime.region_notes_beginner: Skip lime outdoors almost everywhere in this region. It is hurt by cold more easily than any other common citrus, damaged practically at the freezing point, so even the Las Vegas Valley is too cold for it. Only the warmest Laughlin corner gives a protected container lime a real chance, and even there it needs to come fully indoors on cold nights.
lime.region_notes_seasoned: Lime is the clearest no in this region's citrus lineup for anywhere but its single mildest corner. It is the least cold-hardy of the common citrus, with wood and fruit damage in even the hardier Persian (Tahiti) type starting near 32°F, essentially the freezing point itself. The region's cooler zone-8 pockets and, notably, the Las Vegas Valley floor (zone 9) itself both see ordinary winter lows well below that threshold; University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) documents the valley running colder at night than the Phoenix low desert, where lime is already the most cold-exposed citrus grown. Only the Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10), the region's mildest pocket, sits close enough to lime's threshold for a well-protected container tree to survive, and even there it is not a fruiting planting. A container tree moved fully indoors on any freeze night is the only viable way to grow lime anywhere in this belt.
lime.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 30 to 40°F in the mild Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) to 20 to 30°F in the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) to 10 to 20°F in the region's cooler, higher pockets (zone 8), all at or below lime's roughly 32°F wood- and fruit-damage point except at the mildest zone-10 edge. Lime is the least cold-tolerant of the common citrus and has no cold-hardy selection comparable to Meyer lemon or satsuma mandarin; University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) documents this region's winter nights running colder than the Phoenix low desert floor.
lime.cold_basis_beginner: Lime is hurt by cold more easily than almost any other citrus, and this region's winters, even in the Las Vegas Valley itself, routinely get cold enough to kill it. Only the warmest Laughlin corner gives it a real chance, and even there it needs protection.

orange-navel.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 8's cooler, higher pockets bring winter lows well below navel orange's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and its roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point. There is no dependable in-ground establishment window this far into the region's cold edge.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Too cold here for an orange tree outside. Winters regularly drop past the point that damages the tree and freezes the fruit.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: A hard freeze most winters in this zone is well past navel's cold tolerance.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley floor sits close to navel orange's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and its roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point; University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) notes valley winter nights run colder than the Phoenix low desert floor, where navel fruits reliably, so this crop does not clone that warmer verdict here. A container tree brought fully under cover on hard-freeze nights can persist for years and may bloom in a mild winter, but there is no dependable in-ground or fruiting crop; orange sits between the hardier mandarin and the more cold-sensitive grapefruit and lemon in how it handles this valley's winters.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Orange is a middle-of-the-road case here: better cold tolerance than grapefruit or lemon, but the Las Vegas Valley still runs too cold most winters for a dependable in-ground tree. A container tree brought under cover on the coldest nights can survive for years and might fruit in an unusually mild one, but do not count on it.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The valley's frost season (last freeze around Feb 28, first around Nov 25, NWS Las Vegas normals) brackets a winter whose harder nights reach past navel's mid-20s°F wood point and 26°F fruit-freeze point in most years.

10.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after hard-freeze risk passes)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Laughlin/Colorado River corner has the summer heat for good navel quality and sits close enough to its cold edge that fruit is realistic most years: ordinary winter lows here mostly clear the mid-20s°F wood point and the roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point. This is still the region's single mildest, smallest zone with no dedicated local citrus field data, so a hard freeze in a harder winter can still take the crop; protect fruit and young trees when one threatens.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin is warm enough for orange to actually fruit in most years, unlike the rest of this region. It is still a desert winter, so protect the tree and fruit on the occasional hard-freeze night.
10.harvest: Dec - Feb (protect fruit and young trees in a hard freeze)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional hard freeze can still reach navel's mid-25 to mid-26°F damage range even in this mildest zone; protect fruit and young trees on those nights.

orange-navel.region_notes_beginner: Orange lands in the middle of this region's citrus picture: worse than mandarin's cold tolerance, better than grapefruit's or lemon's. It is a protected container prospect in the Las Vegas Valley, and only at the warmest Laughlin corner does it actually fruit most years, with protection on hard freeze nights.
orange-navel.region_notes_seasoned: Navel orange is intermediate in this region's citrus lineup: hardier than grapefruit or lemon, less hardy than mandarin. The region's cooler zone-8 pockets rule it out entirely. The Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) sits close to navel's mid-20s°F wood-damage point and roughly 26°F fruit-freeze point; University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) notes valley winter nights run colder than the Phoenix low desert floor where navel fruits reliably, so this crop stays a protected container specimen there, not a dependable fruiting tree. Only the Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10), the region's mildest pocket, clears that threshold closely enough for real, if freeze-exposed, fruit most years. Ample summer heat is never the constraint anywhere in the region; winter cold is.
orange-navel.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 30 to 40°F in the mild Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) to 20 to 30°F in the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) to 10 to 20°F in the region's cooler, higher pockets (zone 8). Navel orange takes wood damage near the mid-20s°F and fruit damage near 26°F; only zone 10 sits reliably above that band. University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) documents Las Vegas Valley winter nights running colder than the Phoenix low desert floor, the reason navel is judged more cold-limited here than in Arizona's low desert.
orange-navel.cold_basis_beginner: Winters here get cold enough in most of the region to damage an orange tree and freeze the fruit. The warm Laughlin corner is the exception, where the tree usually clears winter and can fruit, with protection on the hardest-freeze nights.
orange-navel.heat_basis_seasoned: The Nevada high desert's long, hot, dry summer, routinely above 90 to 100°F (University of Nevada, Reno Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), banks ample heat for good navel quality; heat is not the limiter anywhere in this region. Winter cold is what keeps the crop to a protected container in most of the belt and a freeze-watched in-ground tree at its warmest corner.
orange-navel.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers are hot enough for good oranges wherever the tree can get through winter. Cold, not heat, is the deciding factor here.

mandarin-clementine.region_label: Nevada: Mojave High Desert (Las Vegas Valley)

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Mandarin, specifically satsuma-type mandarin, is the cold-hardiness standout among the common sweet citrus, but even it cannot take this zone's coldest nights: zone 8's cooler, higher pockets drop well below satsuma's roughly 24°F cold limit in an ordinary winter. There is no dependable in-ground establishment window this far into the region's cold edge.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Even the toughest common citrus, satsuma mandarin, cannot reliably take this zone's coldest nights. Grow it in a pot you bring under cover for winter.
8.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Ordinary winter lows in this zone regularly reach below satsuma's own roughly 24°F cold limit, the hardiest common citrus option.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The Las Vegas Valley floor sits close to satsuma-type mandarin's own roughly 24°F cold limit, the mildest threshold of any citrus in this batch. University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) notes the valley runs colder at night than the Phoenix low desert, where mandarin fruits reliably, so this crop does not earn that warmer verdict here. A container tree brought fully under cover on hard-freeze nights can survive for years and may bloom and set fruit in a mild winter, but there is no dependable in-ground or fruiting crop, only a protected specimen.
9.suitability_note_beginner: This is the best cold-hardiness story among the citrus in this region: satsuma mandarin, the toughest common citrus for cold, can survive in the Las Vegas Valley for years if you protect it on the coldest nights. It still is not safe to leave outside unprotected all winter, and do not count on a reliable harvest; a mild year might give you fruit.
9.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The valley's frost season (last freeze around Feb 28, first around Nov 25, NWS Las Vegas normals) brackets a winter whose harder nights sit right at satsuma's roughly 24°F cold limit in most years.

10.plant_out: Spring (container or balled; after hard-freeze risk passes)
10.suitability_note_seasoned: The Laughlin/Colorado River corner, the region's mildest pocket, gives mandarin its best case: ordinary winter lows here clear satsuma-type mandarin's roughly 24°F cold limit, and early ripening lets the crop come off before the hardest winter cold arrives. This is still the region's single smallest zone with no dedicated local citrus field data, so a harder-than-usual freeze can still cost the crop; protect young trees and pick promptly ahead of any hard freeze.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Laughlin is warm enough that mandarin, especially the early-ripening satsuma type, actually fruits in most years, unlike the rest of the region. Protect young trees on the coldest nights and pick before a hard freeze arrives.
10.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma and early types; pick promptly before hard freezes)
10.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An occasional harder freeze can still reach past satsuma's roughly 24°F cold limit even in this mildest zone; protect young trees and harvest ripe fruit ahead of a hard freeze.

mandarin-clementine.region_notes_beginner: Mandarin is the best cold-hardiness story among this region's citrus. Even so, only a protected container tree makes it through winter in the Las Vegas Valley, with fruit only a mild-year bonus. At the warmest Laughlin corner, an early-ripening satsuma or clementine actually fruits most years if you protect it and pick before the hardest freezes.
mandarin-clementine.region_notes_seasoned: Mandarin, specifically satsuma-type mandarin, is the cold-hardiness standout among the common sweet citrus in this region, and that shows here: the region's cooler zone-8 pockets still fall below its roughly 24°F cold limit and rule the crop out entirely. The Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) sits right at that limit; University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) notes valley winter nights run colder than the Phoenix low desert floor where mandarin fruits reliably, so here it stays a protected container specimen that may bloom in a mild year rather than a dependable in-ground or fruiting tree. Only the Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) clears that cold limit reliably enough, combined with satsuma's early ripening ahead of the hardest cold, for a real, if freeze-watched, crop most years. Summer heat is never the constraint anywhere in this region; winter cold decides the case.
mandarin-clementine.cold_basis_seasoned: Winter lows run from roughly 30 to 40°F in the mild Laughlin/Colorado River corner (zone 10) to 20 to 30°F in the Las Vegas Valley (zone 9) to 10 to 20°F in the region's cooler, higher pockets (zone 8). Satsuma-type mandarin, the hardiest commonly grown sweet citrus, tolerates mature-wood cold to roughly 24°F, close to the valley's edge and reliably cleared only at the mild zone-10 corner. University of Nevada, Reno Extension field observation (SP-20-07) documents this region's winter nights running colder than the Phoenix low desert floor.
mandarin-clementine.cold_basis_beginner: Mandarin takes cold better than any other common citrus, and it can survive in the Las Vegas Valley with real winter protection. Only the warmer Laughlin corner is reliably mild enough for it to actually fruit most years; the region's cooler high pockets are still too cold for it.
mandarin-clementine.heat_basis_seasoned: The Nevada high desert's long, hot, dry summer, routinely above 90 to 100°F (University of Nevada, Reno Cooperative Extension FS-02-61), banks ample heat to sweeten mandarin fruit wherever the tree clears winter; heat is never the limiting factor here. Winter cold, not summer heat, is what keeps this crop to a protected container in most of the region and a freeze-watched in-ground tree only at its warmest corner.
mandarin-clementine.heat_basis_beginner: Our summers here are plenty hot for mandarin fruit to taste good. The reason this is not a reliable outdoor crop across most of the region is winter cold, not a lack of summer warmth.
